extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, breeders, evolutionary biologists and educated readers of Nature (1872)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and reasoning about inheritance: distinguishing patent vs latent elements, modes of representation (class vs family), limits on transmission, and conditions that affect varietal stability and observed resemblance. Useful for scientists and breeders forming or testing hereditary hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish patent (visible) and latent (hidden) elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Out of the structureless ovum embryonic elements develop into the visible adult individual (patent elements), while the large residue is developed into the latent elements contained in the adult individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly separate visible adult traits from latent constituents when explaining inheritance; expect that contributions from latent elements form the major stream of heredity while patent elements contribute relatively little. Use this distinction to interpret breeding outcomes and reversion phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation level: class representation vs family representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Embryonic elements (from the ovum) may be taken by Class Representation, but contributions from an adult's (specialised) patent elements cannot be 'by Class' and are better described as occurring by 'Family Representation'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modelling transmission, decide whether representatives are drawn from broad classes (class representation) or narrower family-like subsets (family representation). Do not assume universal class-level representation when adult elements are specialised; use family-level sampling to explain observed trait transmission patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ovum capacity limits force representative (not exhaustive) transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: The large variety of adult latent elements cannot all be transmitted because no two parents are exactly alike and the accumulation of sub-varieties over generations would exceed what could be packed into a single ovum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat contributions from parents to offspring as representative samples of familial variation rather than as full copies of parental repertoires. Explanations and models must account for combinatorial/packing limits of gametes and therefore expect sampling effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal (visible) manifestation usually indicates latent equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Many cases that appear to be purely personal characteristics really belong to personal traits conjoined with latent equivalents; the personal manifestation is on the average a certain proof of the existence of some latent elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a trait first appears visibly in an individual, avoid concluding latent elements are absent; use cross-breeding and domestication evidence (e.g., spots/bars breedable into domestic varieties) to infer underlying latent elements are widespread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical expectation for inheritance when both parents show trait (~one-quarter rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Breeders, when they mate two animals each having the same unusual characteristic (not necessarily by known hereditary transmission), would consider themselves fortunate if one quarter of the progeny inherited that quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use breeder statistics as rough expectations: concordant parents produce minority proportion of affected offspring (~25%) on average, consistent with representative latent contributions. Lower ratios are expected if latent elements are absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversion indicates strong transmission of latent elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The large transmission of purely latent elements can be shown by the well-known facts of reversion; latent-only cases (case 3) produce reversion phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reversion (ancestral traits reappearing after one or more generations) as evidence that latent elements are transmitted broadly even when not phenotypically expressed; include reversion in models of hidden inheritance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urn-sampling analogy for segregation and unpredictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Inheritance may be pictured by an urn containing many marked balls: a handful drawn at random represents a parent's person; combining samples from two parents and redrawing yields an offspring sample — the nearer connection between parent and child is thus sampling-based and can be very remote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use random-sampling analogies (urn model) to reason about variation, resemblance, and unpredictability of offspring: high diversity in the 'urn' (structureless elements) yields unpredictable embryos; low diversity yields resemblance (purity of blood). Apply sampling/statistical thinking to heredity claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedigree-only reasoning: true hereditary link is between primary elements in ova
rubrics_metrics.description: It is fallacious to reckon inheritance in the popular way from parents to offspring (visible personalities). The true hereditary link connects the primary elements as they existed in the newly impregnated ova from which individuals were developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In theoretical and empirical heredity work, focus on gametic/ovular composition and primary elements rather than only on adult phenotypes or ordinary pedigrees; pedigrees alone add confusion without addressing underlying element composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of blood and unchanged developmental conditions required for stable varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: If the structureless elements are not diverse (i.e., purity of blood is fulfilled) the offspring will resemble its parents; a variety cannot be stable unless the conditions of development concur to maintain the structureless stages of consecutive generations in an unchanged form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of stable breed/type by checking both genetic 'purity' (low diversity in structureless elements) and environmental/developmental consistency across generations. Breeders' selected stocks may fail to remain true if reared under different conditions (feralization example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in adult habits can induce sterility via increased gametic variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in the habits of life after adult age is reached are apt to produce sterility; many grains of pollen or many spermatozoa are required to fertilise each ovum because each separate one may not contain a sufficiently complete representation of primary elements, implying variation in gametes and ova that can be increased by habit changes to the point of sterility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing fertility or sterility phenomena, consider behavioral/environmental shifts in adults as factors that increase variance in gametic constituents. Expect fertility to depend on accumulation of representative elements from multiple gametes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of individual variation are locatable to segregation, sampling, and developmental stages
rubrics_metrics.description: If structureless elements are diverse, the embryo character is unpredictable; segregation and selection of embryonic vs latent elements may cause inheritance to skip alternate generations; removal of material for embryonic development reduces latent pool, affecting subsequent manifestation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining individual variation or generation-skipping inheritance, map causes to (a) diversity in the structureless pool (sampling), (b) which elements are allocated to embryonic development versus latent residue, and (c) developmental/environmental influences. Use these stages to sort observed variation into proper causal categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large individual variation (including intellectual/moral) is compatible with heredity in mongrelised populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Large variation in individuals from their parents is not incompatible with heredity but is a consequence of it wherever the breed is impure; human intellectual and moral gifts show great individual variation under present (highly mongrelised) conditions, and averages are the relevant measure to demonstrate inheritance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use high individual variation as evidence against hereditary transmission of complex traits; instead, use statistical averages across populations to assess heritability, particularly in admixed/mongrelised populations.
